name: Tomas Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies or government. This is confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, with a master’s and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I lead reviews at a small accounting firm. I check accounts and tax returns, chase missing invoices, and enjoy finding a wrong figure before a client signs. Repeated late corrections from clients wear me down near the filing deadline.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, outside the figures?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The salary is low for this job, yet I am the person juniors bring hard files to. I have less than one month of expenses saved, and there are few similar jobs near my flat. I prefer the methods I know and have never used AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team the little checks might get quicker, but clients will still want a person to sign the returns. Our firm still has to explain mistakes face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our pay is already low for qualified accountants, and my savings would not cover one month. Even a quiet patch worries me more than an AI headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reviewing accounts and tax returns in the same order, and ask my manager for the next six months of client work. Starting now I would stop ordering lunch out twice a week and put that money against my overdraft; in the first year of this picture I would keep that routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel tired of pretending the rent is easy, though the work itself feels familiar. A small software change is not the part keeping me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a normal day look like when you say you keep the routine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check the ledger totals, ring clients about missing invoices, and review the junior staff’s tax calculations. I like catching an error before a client sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the next month is light?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lunch bought near the office goes first, about 40 a month. I would not cut the train fare because there are few accounting firms near my flat.

say: I would say **client sign-off** still needs an accountant even if routine checks speed up.
I would tell colleagues our **firm** still answers for errors in tax returns.
think: I know my **low pay** leaves almost no room for a quiet month.
I worry more about the **overdraft** than about small changes to accounting software.
do: Keep reviewing **client accounts** and ask my manager about six months of work.
Stop buying **office lunches** twice weekly and reduce my overdraft.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about money while the work still feels familiar.
S0.quote: Our pay is already low for qualified accountants, and my savings would not cover one month.
fieldNote: His **professional confidence** is real: he enjoys finding ledger errors and expects clients to value accountable sign-off.
His **thin cushion** makes an ordinary slow month threatening, even while this scenario leaves the shape of work largely intact.

steps.text: Keep reviewing client accounts and ask manager about six months of work
Stop buying office lunch twice weekly and reduce overdraft

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say firms should check what the software gets wrong before they cut people. Our clients send messy records, and someone has to own the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking are most of my desk day, so I could lose hours even as the lead reviewer. If a junior vacancy disappears first, I will know my turn may come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the partners for a written plan on which accounts and tax reviews stay with our team. I would keep using our approved spreadsheet checks, but I would not try a new AI tool without training; in the first year I would save the lunch money and ask about any vacant compliance post at the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious when I picture an empty desk left unfilled. Being good at the job does not create another firm nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if a junior desk stayed empty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my manager whether the work has moved into software or onto the rest of us. I would not tell the juniors everything is safe when I do not know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a compliance post rather than a new firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compliance means checking whether rules are followed, and I already do parts of it for tax work. There are few nearby accounting jobs, and I cannot fund a long job search.

say: I would insist on **checking errors** before our firm cuts accounting staff.
I would tell clients a **person** still owns the final tax return.
think: I expect routine **writing and checking** to take hours from my desk work.
I would read an **unfilled junior vacancy** as a warning about my own job.
do: Ask partners for a **written work plan** and keep using approved spreadsheet checks.
Save the **lunch money** and ask about a vacant compliance role inside the firm.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fewer hours and scarce local alternatives.
S1.quote: Being good at the job does not create another firm nearby.
fieldNote: He frames his public concern as **quality control**, which fits his strength in reviewing messy client records.
Privately, an **unfilled junior desk** is his measure of exposure; he lacks savings for a long external search.

steps.text: Keep using approved spreadsheet checks on client accounts
Put former lunch spending against overdraft each month
Ask about vacant compliance posts within the accounting firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches our tax and accounts screens straight away. Robots arriving around 2031 do not give this desk job three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am good at spotting mistakes, but cheaper thinking work could do nearly all my review by 2028. I cannot make less than one month of savings stretch through an uncertain job hunt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the partners if they will pay for training in tax disputes and client representation, where a human may still be wanted. If they approve fees and paid time in writing, I would enroll in the short course before 2028. I would cut paid lunches and my streaming subscription immediately; if my hours fall in the first year after 2028, I would apply to the firm’s compliance vacancy if one exists and ask my sister for a temporary room before missing rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, and the short clock makes my chest tight. I do not have an independent plan that could replace this salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell clients their returns are safe with the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the firm remains responsible for every return, whatever makes the first draft. I would not promise that my own desk survives 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you call your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call my sister only after a written cut in hours, not over a rumour. She has a spare room, but I would feel ashamed asking.

say: I would say **AGI by 2028** reaches our tax and accounts screens immediately.
I would remind colleagues that **client responsibility** stays with the firm.
think: I expect cheaper thinking work could replace most of my **review hours** by 2028.
I cannot support a long job hunt with **less than a month** saved.
do: Ask partners for **written funding**, then enroll in tax dispute training before 2028.
Cancel paid lunches and **streaming** now; seek a compliance vacancy if hours fall.
Ask my **sister** for a temporary room after a written hours cut.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely income loss and a two-year deadline.
S2.quote: Robots arriving around 2031 do not give this desk job three extra years.
fieldNote: The **robot delay** offers him no comfort because his valuable tasks are almost entirely thinking work at a screen.
His training idea depends on **partner funding**; housing help depends on a written hours cut, showing how little money he can risk.

steps.text: Enroll in tax dispute course if partners approve fees and paid time in writing
Cancel office lunches and streaming subscription immediately
Apply for a vacant firm compliance post if hours fall
Ask sister for temporary room after written hours cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to sort out a sensible handover. The firm should spell out who checks the client’s final figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me pay off the overdraft, but I still expect software to threaten my desk work when 2031 arrives. The robots in 2034 matter less to my tax returns than the earlier thinking system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the partners whether they would fund a short course in tax disputes next year, then enrol if they agree in writing to fees and paid time away from accounts, and practise speaking with clients about contested assessments. I would save 80 a month after the overdraft is cleared, if my hours stay full; in the first year after 2031, I would seek a client representation opening at this firm if one is vacant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years sounds like a calendar I can actually use. I would still hate relying on a promise from the partners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need the course fees and time away from accounts agreed before enrolling. With my savings, I cannot pay first and hope to be reimbursed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if there is no opening in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the accounts team while it has hours and ask for a list of nearby firms then. There are few, so I will not resign ahead of a vacancy.

say: I would ask for a **clear handover** and named responsibility for final client figures.
I would say the **2031 deadline** gives our firm time to plan.
think: I still expect **desk work** to shrink when AGI arrives in 2031.
I can clear my **overdraft** before then if my hours hold.
do: Enroll in **tax dispute training** next year if partners approve fees and paid time in writing.
Save **80 monthly** after clearing the overdraft, if my hours stay full.
Apply for a vacant **client representation** role after 2031; otherwise keep accounts hours.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though five years gives me a usable schedule.
S3.quote: With my savings, I cannot pay first and hope to be reimbursed.
fieldNote: He will test a new direction only with **written funding**, consistent with his reluctance to gamble on unfamiliar work.
His **vacancy condition** matters: he will keep account-review hours rather than resign on the strength of a speculative opening.

steps.text: Enroll in tax dispute course next year if partners approve fees and paid time
Save 80 monthly after clearing overdraft if hours stay full
Apply for vacant client representation role after 2031
Keep reviewing accounts if no new role opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the firm a decade is long enough to build a better service around clients, even if AGI writes and checks returns by 2036. We should not pretend the robots in 2039 change our deadlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me time to become the person clients trust with disputes, but I cannot assume that job will still pay well. My low salary now makes the long wait feel less comfortable than it sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would clear the overdraft and ask for partner-funded dispute training, one course at a time. I would enrol in the first course only once the partners approve fees and paid time in writing. I would aim for three months of expenses in savings by 2031, if my hours stay full; in the first year after 2036, I would keep a client-facing post if the firm offers one and otherwise apply for a vacant compliance job without quitting first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel guarded but less trapped than with 2028. My worry is that I spend ten years preparing for a role that disappears too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the client-facing work is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to sit in on dispute meetings and count whether clients pay for our help. I am not changing my title on a brochure and calling it security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your younger self about this path?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my younger self that the chartered qualification opened a door, but a title cannot pay next month’s rent. I need savings before I take even a sensible risk.

say: I would say **ten years** lets the firm build client help around tax disputes.
I would remind colleagues our **desk deadline** is 2036, before hands-on robots arrive.
think: I could build **client trust**, but the future pay for that work is uncertain.
My **low salary** makes saving enough for a change difficult.
do: Clear the **overdraft** and enroll in each dispute course after written partner approval of fees and paid time.
Build **three months** of expenses in savings by 2031 if my hours stay full.
Keep a **client-facing post** after 2036 or apply for a vacant compliance role.
feel: I feel **guarded**, with enough time to make a plan.
S4.quote: I am not changing my title on a brochure and calling it security.
fieldNote: He wants **observable client demand** before trusting a new title, which shows both professional judgment and caution about technology.
The **ten-year runway** eases urgency, but low pay and a thin starting cushion still shape his risk of lost income.

steps.text: Build three months of expenses by 2031 if hours stay full
Enroll in each dispute course only with written approval of fees and paid time
Keep client-facing firm post after 2036 if offered
Apply for vacant compliance role if firm post ends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my review work could go before I have even one month of rent saved. A paid course and honest notice about hours from the partners would help more than a speech about adapting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I can afford to be wrong once. I cannot. My chartered title looks solid on a door, but next month’s rent still comes out of this month’s pay.

headlineQuote: My chartered title looks solid on a door, but next month’s rent still comes out of this month’s pay.
portrait: At **27**, Tomas leads account and tax reviews at a small firm and is trusted with the hardest files.
His **master’s and chartered qualification** sit beside low pay, less than one month saved, and few nearby accounting jobs.
He has **never used AI** and prefers familiar methods; he asks for funded training before trying tax dispute work.
The **2028 deadline** alarms him because thinking AI reaches his desk immediately, while longer runways let him save and seek internal roles.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his account-review hours before he can save even one month of rent.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid training** in tax disputes and honest advance notice about hours from the firm’s partners.
